at.step: Local search, defined on the problem it is famous on: a closed tour visiting every point once. A neighborhood is every tour one small change away. Two-opt removes two edges and reconnects the other way, reversing the segment between them — the move that uncrosses a crossing tour.

Here is the honest measurement, not an assumption: twelve points, their true shortest tour found by checking every possibility exactly. Run two-opt from a hundred different random starting tours, and it stops at that true optimum well under half the time.

Two-opt always stops. It never says where. Before the next technique's own numbers: would a search that is sometimes willing to accept a worse move actually escape a local optimum like this one, or would it just wander randomly and never settle anywhere at all?

Simulated annealing: accept a worse move with a probability that falls as a temperature is lowered, following Kirkpatrick, Gelatt and Vecchi's own rule from 1983. Measured on the identical twelve-point instance, it reaches the true optimum far more often than plain two-opt — a measured result, not an assumed one.

A genetic search: a population of candidate tours, selection by fitness, crossover combining two parents, mutation. Run on the identical instance with this topic's own implementation, it actually does worse than plain two-opt — not because genetic algorithms are weak in general, but because no fixed ranking holds among these searches.

syllabus.clause: when heuristics without guarantees are the right engineering call (PostgreSQL's GEQO for many-way joins)

at.step: PostgreSQL's own documentation names the real system doing exactly this. Below a threshold, it searches every join order exhaustively. At or above it, a genetic algorithm takes over: a join tree becomes an integer string, two strings cross over into a child, and mutation is deprecated outright so no repair step is ever needed.

One query runs once an hour. Another runs ten thousand times a second. Both would cross the threshold where the exhaustive planner becomes too slow. Which one should the documented genetic planner actually be trusted on?

Its own documentation admits the fit is imperfect: a traveling-salesman tour's cost per piece doesn't depend on the rest of the tour, but a join order's cost does. The honest engineering call: give up the worst-case guarantee only where the exhaustive search's own cost is the bigger risk, and say so plainly.

items.item: Local search's absence of a guarantee is not a weaker guarantee — it is the literal absence of one. Unlike the approximation ratios of earlier topics in this chapter, no number bounds how far a two-opt local optimum can be from the true optimum in general; this topic states that absence directly rather than quietly implying some unstated bound exists.

at.step: Here is the honest measurement, not an assumption: twelve points, their true shortest tour found by checking every possibility exactly. Run two-opt from a hundred different random starting tours, and it stops at that true optimum well under half the time.

items.item: The measured ranking (annealing better than two-opt, this genetic algorithm worse than two-opt) is a fact about one instance, one random seed, and one set of algorithm settings — not a general law about these three families of search. A different cooling schedule, population size, or problem instance could change every one of these numbers, and the topic does not claim otherwise.

at.step: A genetic search: a population of candidate tours, selection by fitness, crossover combining two parents, mutation. Run on the identical instance with this topic's own implementation, it actually does worse than plain two-opt — not because genetic algorithms are weak in general, but because no fixed ranking holds among these searches.

items.item: The genetic algorithm measured in this topic is the builder's own simple implementation on a travelling-salesman tour, not PostgreSQL's actual GEQO, which operates on join-order trees with the real query planner's own cost estimate as its fitness function — the two are related by analogy, not identity, and this topic's measured numbers describe only its own implementation.

PostgreSQL's geqo_threshold interacts with from_collapse_limit and join_collapse_limit, which bound how much of a query the planner merges into one join problem before either search even runs; a query under the FROM-item threshold can still reach the genetic planner if these collapse limits are set low enough to push it there, so threshold alone does not fully decide which planner runs.

Simulated annealing's acceptance rule depends on a temperature schedule (how fast the temperature falls) that is itself a design choice with no universally correct answer; this topic uses one geometric schedule and states the specific constants used, rather than implying the measured result holds for every possible schedule.

at.step: Simulated annealing: accept a worse move with a probability that falls as a temperature is lowered, following Kirkpatrick, Gelatt and Vecchi's own rule from 1983. Measured on the identical twelve-point instance, it reaches the true optimum far more often than plain two-opt — a measured result, not an assumed one.

items.item: The travelling salesman problem is NP-hard, which this topic states but does not re-derive (it is declared, inherited from the chapter's NP-hardness thread) — the exact twelve-point optimum shown here is found only because twelve points is small enough for exhaustive dynamic programming to finish, not because the problem has become easy in general.

items.item: The predict question about query frequency and geqo_threshold has a real asymmetry baked into PostgreSQL's own trade-off: planning cost is paid once per execution, so a query executed constantly amplifies any planning-time saving or plan-quality loss far more than a rarely run one — the topic's explanation names this mechanism directly rather than treating the answer as obvious.

at.step: One query runs once an hour. Another runs ten thousand times a second. Both would cross the threshold where the exhaustive planner becomes too slow. Which one should the documented genetic planner actually be trusted on?

items.item: Two-opt's neighborhood (reversing one segment) is a strict subset of k-opt's larger neighborhoods (reconnecting k edges at once); a wider neighborhood can only ever find a local optimum at least as good as a narrower one on the same instance, which is why the syllabus clause names both, even though this topic's measurements use only two-opt — the topic does not claim two-opt's own measured numbers would hold for three-opt or larger neighborhoods.

items.item: The twelve-point instance's clustering (four loose groups of three points) is a deliberate choice, not an arbitrary one: points spread uniformly at random over a square gave two-opt a near-certain chance of finding the true optimum in early testing, which would not have demonstrated the chapter's point about local search's missing guarantee at all.

This topic's exact optimum is found by the Held-Karp dynamic program over subsets, which runs in exponential time itself (the state space doubles with every added point); it is exact only because twelve points keeps that exponential small enough to finish, not because the method scales to realistic instance sizes.
